profile.reading:
Switch operates its Atlanta-metro campus, branded "The Keep Campus," at 1 Switch Way, Lithia Springs, Georgia 30122, in Douglas County west of downtown Atlanta; Switch's own Atlanta page does not name Lithia Springs directly, but this OSM record's address tags place it there specifically. Switch's current marketing describes The Keep as a 2,000-plus acre expansion campus with up to 1 million square feet of data center space and up to 150 megawatts of power at this stage, positioned toward "multi-gigawatt capacity upon completion" as the campus continues to build out. Switch announced the Atlanta campus in May 2017, and a November 2020 press release describing an anchor-tenant signing and groundbreaking on the next two buildings gave more granular figures: Building 2 targeted to come online in 2022 at 50 megawatts, and Building 3 targeted for 2023 at 35 megawatts, alongside a stated "$2.5 billion" total expected Georgia investment and hundreds of expected jobs. Switch names Georgia Power by name as its utility partner, describing "100 percent green energy from new, local and renewable energy resources" delivered through that partnership. Georgia Governor Nathan Deal signed House Bill 696, informally called the "Switch Bill," in May 2018, which modernized Georgia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption to extend it to hyperscale colocation facilities with a minimum $250 million investment, a legislative change Switch's own materials credit as enabling this Georgia expansion; Switch's current site states a 0 percent sales and use tax position in Georgia as a result. Switch markets the campus under its self-created "Tier 5 Platinum" certification standard rather than an Uptime Institute Tier rating.

Georgia's data center sector has expanded well beyond the Atlanta metro's historic technology and telecommunications base, with Douglas County's position along Interstate 20 west of Atlanta offering large parcels of developable industrial land and proximity to Georgia Power's regional transmission infrastructure, factors that have drawn Switch and other large-scale operators to the area. Georgia Power's own long-range integrated resource planning has increasingly cited data center and other large-load growth as a driver of future generation and transmission investment across its Georgia service territory, a dynamic playing out alongside the state's continued use of its 2018 data center sales-tax exemption expansion to attract hyperscale-scale investment like Switch's Keep Campus.

Switch Las Vegas 10 sits at 7375 Lindell Road, Las Vegas, Nevada, on Switch's Core Campus in unincorporated Clark County. Switch opened the building June 15, 2017, built using Switch's modular "MOD 250" construction design, roughly 350,000 square feet with up to 40 megawatts of power capacity. Switch's own opening press release states the building was constructed by a workforce of roughly 1,000 workers, 85 percent Nevada residents, over an eight-month build period, and that at the time of opening the Core Campus's three largest buildings together, Las Vegas 8, 9, and 10, totaled more than 2 million square feet and up to 315 megawatts of power. Switch's own materials place construction of Las Vegas 10 alongside the neighboring Las Vegas 11 building, together adding roughly 700,000 combined square feet to the campus. Switch markets its Core Campus today as offering up to 495 megawatts of power upon completion, a figure that has grown substantially from the 315 megawatts stated at Las Vegas 10's 2017 opening, reflecting continued campus buildout including newer AI-focused buildings. Switch does not state a formal Uptime Institute Tier certification for Las Vegas 10 specifically; the campus overall has marketed its self-created "Tier 5 Platinum" standard since 2017. Switch's Nevada tax-advantages materials describe a consumer-use-tax abatement to as low as 2 percent and a 75 percent property-tax abatement for customer equipment, administered through Nevada's Governor's Office of Economic Development, and Switch states 100 percent renewable energy sourcing across its Nevada campuses.

Las Vegas 10's modular "MOD 250" construction approach reflected a broader industry shift toward prefabricated, factory-assembled data center components intended to compress build timelines; Switch's own press materials specifically credited the modular design with enabling the roughly eight-month construction period. Clark County's data center cluster, anchored substantially by Switch's Core Campus, has helped establish Las Vegas as a significant secondary U.S. data center market, drawing additional colocation and hyperscale investment from other operators over the past decade beyond Switch alone.

profile.reading:
Switch: The Rock sits on Switch's Round Rock, Texas campus, at Dell Technologies' global headquarters address in Williamson County, part of the Austin metro. Switch announced the Texas campus, its fifth "PRIME" development, on June 2, 2021, naming it "The Rock" and simultaneously agreeing to acquire Data Foundry, a two-decades-established Austin and Houston colocation operator, contributing more than 500,000 square feet and 60 megawatts of existing capacity to the combined Texas footprint. Switch's own materials state The Rock campus alone offers more than 1.5 million square feet of data center space, with the full Texas ecosystem, Rock plus the acquired Data Foundry sites, exceeding 2 million square feet and a stated 185 megawatts of total capacity at the time of the 2021 announcement. Switch does not publish this site's exact street address, campus acreage, or a confirmed opening date; the popular association of "The Rock" name with a former limestone quarry does not appear anywhere in Switch's own published materials and is not confirmed here. An August 2026 Switch statement responding to Texas Governor Greg Abbott's data center standards discloses that Switch has committed more than $250 million in local investment under a long-term economic development agreement with the City of Round Rock generating tax revenue through 2037, and pledges cooperation with ERCOT, the Public Utility Commission of Texas, and local communities on noise mitigation, lighting controls, setbacks, and traffic improvements. Switch markets the campus under its self-created "Tier 5" branding rather than an Uptime Institute Tier certification, and states 100 percent renewable energy sourced through renewable energy credit purchases rather than direct on-site generation.

Round Rock and the broader Williamson County area have drawn substantial technology-sector investment beyond Switch, including major semiconductor manufacturing nearby, part of a broader Central Texas corridor stretching from Austin through Georgetown and Taylor that has become one of the fastest-growing U.S. technology and advanced-manufacturing regions over the past decade. Switch's Data Foundry acquisition, folded into the Rock campus's combined Texas capacity figures, gave Switch an immediate operating presence in both Austin and Houston rather than requiring it to build out Texas capacity entirely from scratch.

reading:
Switch is a private data center operator headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada. DigitalBridge Investment Management and IFM Investors announced a take-private acquisition of Switch in May 2022 for approximately $11 billion, completed later that year, after which Switch ceased to be an independent SEC filer.

The company's own site describes more than 26 years of operations and names five exascale campus locations, Tahoe Reno, Las Vegas, Atlanta, Grand Rapids, and Austin/Houston, without stating a precise founding year, founder, or current aggregate capacity figure beyond a general claim of modular power density up to gigawatt scale per facility. Switch's Tahoe Reno and Las Vegas campuses in Nevada are among the industry's largest known single-site data center developments, though no square footage or megawatt total for either was located on the operator's site this session.

The registry here tracks 15 Switch facilities across three states, Georgia, Nevada, and Texas, a subset of the five campus markets named on the operator's own site, which additionally lists Michigan (Grand Rapids). No dollar-denominated construction investment figure specific to these states was located this session.
